q: What is a deal called when the acquirer's pro forma EPS is greater than its standalone EPS before the deal?
explain: An accretive deal raises the buyer's post-deal EPS; a dilutive deal lowers it. Pro forma EPS equal to standalone EPS is breakeven.
hook: Accrete = add on; the EPS grows.

sources.title: Accretion Dilution Analysis - Definition, Affect Merger
sources.quote: An accretive acquisition or merger is one where the pro forma (post-deal) Earnings per Share is greater than the acquirer's (buyer's) EPS before the deal is made.

sources.title: Merger Model | M&A Training Tutorial + Excel Template
sources.quote: Accretive Merger → Increase in Pro Forma EPS

q: If an acquirer's standalone EPS is $2.00 and its pro forma EPS is $2.20, what is the percentage EPS accretion?
explain: Accretion/(dilution) = (pro forma EPS / standalone EPS) - 1, so $2.20 / $2.00 - 1 = 10%.
hook: Divide new by old, then subtract one.

sources.title: Merger Model | M&A Training Tutorial + Excel Template
sources.quote: EPS Accretion / (Dilution) = (Pro Forma EPS ÷ Standalone EPS) – 1

q: In the accretion/dilution rule of thumb, the acquirer's after-tax cost of issuing stock equals the reciprocal of which multiple?
explain: The cost of stock is 1 / the buyer's P/E multiple, i.e. the after-tax profit each buyer share generates relative to its price.
hook: Flip the P/E to get the earnings yield.

sources.title: EPS Accretion Dilution – Rules of Thumb for Merger Models
sources.quote: After-Tax Cost of Issuing Stock = 1 / Buyer's P/E Multiple (i.e., take the reciprocal of the buyer's P/E multiple )

q: Using the rule of thumb, what is the cost of stock for an acquirer trading at a P/E multiple of 20x?
explain: Cost of stock = 1 / P/E, so 1 / 20 = 5%.

sources.title: EPS Accretion Dilution – Rules of Thumb for Merger Models
sources.quote: After-Tax Cost of Issuing Stock = 1 / Buyer's P/E Multiple (i.e., take the reciprocal of the buyer's P/E multiple )

q: What is the after-tax cost of new acquisition debt with an 8% interest rate if the buyer's tax rate is 25%?
explain: After-tax cost of debt = interest rate on debt x (1 - buyer's tax rate) = 8% x 75% = 6%.
hook: Interest is tax-deductible, so shave off the tax rate.

sources.title: EPS Accretion Dilution – Rules of Thumb for Merger Models
sources.quote: After-Tax Cost of Debt = Interest Rate on Debt * (1 – Buyer's Tax Rate)

q: In the accretion/dilution rule of thumb, the seller's yield equals the seller's net income divided by what?
explain: Seller's yield = seller's net income / equity purchase price, which is compared against the buyer's weighted cost of acquisition.
hook: Yield = what you earn / what you paid for the equity.

sources.title: EPS Accretion Dilution – Rules of Thumb for Merger Models
sources.quote: Seller's Yield = Seller's Net Income / Equity Purchase Price.

q: If the buyer's weighted cost of acquisition is higher than the seller's yield, is the deal accretive or dilutive?
explain: When the buyer's weighted cost of acquisition exceeds the seller's yield, the deal is dilutive; if the seller's yield is higher, it is accretive.
hook: Paying more than you earn dilutes.

sources.title: EPS Accretion Dilution – Rules of Thumb for Merger Models
sources.quote: If the Weighted Cost of Acquisition is higher than the Seller's Yield, the deal will be dilutive ; otherwise, if the Seller's Yield is higher, it will be accretive .

q: A deal is funded 50% with cash (after-tax cost 3%) and 50% with stock (cost 5%); what is the buyer's weighted cost of acquisition?
explain: Weighted cost = 3% x 50% + 5% x 50% = 4%. Against a seller's yield above 4%, the deal would be accretive.
hook: Halfway between 3 and 5.

sources.title: EPS Accretion Dilution – Rules of Thumb for Merger Models
sources.quote: Weighted Cost of Acquisition = After-Tax Cost of Cash * % Cash Used + After-Tax Cost of Debt * % Debt Used + Cost of Stock * % Stock Used

q: From a financial perspective, which funding source is described as the lowest-cost way for an acquirer to pay for a deal?
explain: Each funding source has a different cost, and acquirers want to use cash, the lowest-cost source, as much as possible.
hook: Cash only gives up a little interest income.

sources.title: Merger Model Tutorials
sources.quote: Each funding source has a different “cost,” so from a financial perspective, acquirers want to use the lowest-cost funding source (Cash) as much as possible.

q: Which income statement metric reflects the full impact of deal financing, including foregone interest on cash, new interest expense and new shares?
explain: EPS = net income / shares outstanding, and net income includes interest income and expense, so EPS captures cash, debt and stock financing effects.
hook: Only EPS sees the share count.

sources.title: Merger Model Tutorials
sources.quote: EPS accretion/dilution is significant because Earnings per Share (EPS) is the only Income Statement metric that reflects the full impact of the deal financing: Foregone Interest Income on Cash Used, Interest Expense on Debt Used, and the additional shares from Stock Issued.

q: Cross-selling each company's products to the other company's customers is an example of which type of synergy?
explain: Revenue synergies are extra revenue the combined company generates beyond what the two firms could separately, e.g. from cross-selling or new markets.
hook: Cross-sell = more sales = revenue.

sources.title: Synergies in M&A | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: Revenue synergies can arise from cross-selling the products of each company to the customers of the other, entering new markets or geographies by utilizing the expanded reach of the combined firm, developing new products by merging capabilities, and increasing prices through enhanced pricing power and market reach.

q: Which type of synergy is generally considered easier to estimate and achieve?
explain: Cost synergies come from eliminating redundancies and are considered easier to estimate and achieve; revenue synergies are more speculative and take longer.
hook: Cutting costs is in your control; customers are not.

sources.title: Synergies in M&A | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: Cost synergies are considered easier to estimate and achieve compared to revenue synergies.

q: Assuming a 60% gross margin, how much pre-tax profit do $10 million of revenue synergies contribute?
explain: Revenue synergies are reduced by the margin assumption before being taxed: $10 million x 60% = $6 million. Cost synergies, by contrast, flow through with only a tax adjustment.
hook: Revenue synergies pay for their own costs first.

sources.title: Synergies in M&A | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: In comparison, revenue synergies are reduced by the margin assumption prior to being taxed.

q: In a taxable asset purchase, what kind of tax basis does the acquirer receive in the acquired net assets?
explain: In a taxable asset purchase, acquired net assets are written up (or down) from the seller's tax basis to fair value on the acquirer's tax balance sheet, creating extra depreciation and amortization deductions.
hook: Buy the assets, step up the basis.

sources.title: Asset and Stock Deals - Examples, Templates | Macabacus
sources.quote: A major tax advantage to the acquirer of structuring a transaction as a taxable asset purchase is that the acquirer receives stepped-up tax basis in the target's net assets (assets minus liabilities).

sources.title: Asset Purchase vs Stock Purchase - Pro/Cons Reasons for Each Type
sources.quote: A major tax advantage is that the buyer can “step up” the basis of many assets over their current tax values and obtain tax deductions for depreciation and/or amortization.

q: In a stock acquisition without a Section 338 election, what tax basis does the buyer take in the target's assets?
explain: In a stock deal the buyer assumes the seller's existing tax basis in the acquired net assets; the target's asset basis stays the same.
hook: Stock deal: the old basis carries over.

sources.title: Asset and Stock Deals - Examples, Templates | Macabacus
sources.quote: The acquirer does not receive a stepped-up tax basis in the acquired net assets but, rather, a carryover basis.

sources.title: S Corp Chapter 16 (California Franchise Tax Board)
sources.quote: The basis of the assets held by the target corporation (now ow­ ned by the new shareholder) stays the same.

q: Over how many years is tax-deductible goodwill from an asset purchase amortized for U.S. tax purposes?
explain: Goodwill from an asset sale or 338 election is tax-deductible and amortized over 15 years under IRC Section 197; goodwill from a plain stock sale is not tax-deductible.
hook: Asset deal goodwill: 15 years of tax shields.

sources.title: Asset and Stock Deals - Examples, Templates | Macabacus
sources.quote: Tax-deductible and amortized over 15 years for tax purposes under IRC Section 197.

sources.title: Goodwill Amortization | GAAP vs. Tax Accounting Criteria
sources.quote: Asset Sale/338 : Any goodwill created in an acquisition structured as an asset sale/338 is tax-deductible and amortizable over 15 years, along with other intangible assets that fall under IRC section 197.

q: Which Internal Revenue Code section governs the 15-year tax amortization of goodwill created in an asset purchase?
explain: Goodwill and other Section 197 intangibles acquired in an asset sale or 338 election are amortized over 15 years for tax purposes.
hook: 197 intangibles, 15 years.

sources.title: Asset and Stock Deals - Examples, Templates | Macabacus
sources.quote: Tax-deductible and amortized over 15 years for tax purposes under IRC Section 197.

sources.title: Goodwill Amortization | GAAP vs. Tax Accounting Criteria
sources.quote: Asset Sale/338 : Any goodwill created in an acquisition structured as an asset sale/338 is tax-deductible and amortizable over 15 years, along with other intangible assets that fall under IRC section 197.

q: A Section 338(h)(10) election treats a stock acquisition as what for U.S. federal income tax purposes?
explain: Section 338 elections let a buyer acquire stock for legal purposes while getting the tax treatment, including the basis step-up, of an asset acquisition.
hook: Legally stock, taxed like assets.

sources.title: Section 338 - What it is, Implications, S Corporation
sources.quote: These elections treat a stock acquisition as an asset acquisition for federal income tax purposes.

sources.title: Section 338(h)(10) Election | Practical Law
sources.quote: An election to treat a stock acquisition of the target corporation generally as an asset acquisition for US federal income tax purposes.

q: A qualified stock purchase (QSP), required for a Section 338 election, requires buying at least what percentage of the target's total voting power and value?
explain: A QSP is the purchase of at least 80% of the total voting power and value of a corporation's stock by another corporation during a 12-month acquisition period.
hook: 338 needs 80.

sources.title: Instructions for Form 8023 (10/2023) | Internal Revenue Service
sources.quote: A QSP is the purchase of at least 80% of the total voting power and value of the stock of a corporation by another corporation during a 12-month acquisition period.

sources.title: Section 338(h)(10) Election | Practical Law
sources.quote: A QSP is the purchase (as defined in IRC § 338(h)(3)) of at least 80% of the total voting power and value of the stock of a corporation by another corporation in a transaction (or series of transactions) during a 12-month acquisition period.

q: If the target is an S corporation, which of its shareholders must make the Section 338(h)(10) election?
explain: For an S corporation target, the 338(h)(10) election must be made by all shareholders, including those who do not sell their stock in the qualified stock purchase.
hook: S corp: everyone signs, sellers or not.

sources.title: Instructions for Form 8023 (10/2023) | Internal Revenue Service
sources.quote: If the target is an S corporation, a section 338(h)(10) election must be made by all of the shareholders of the target, including shareholders who do not sell target stock in the QSP.

sources.title: Section 338 - What it is, Implications, S Corporation
sources.quote: All shareholders of the target S corporation (selling and non-selling) must consent to the election.

q: How many levels of tax does a regular Section 338(g) election impose?
explain: A 338(g) election taxes both the shareholders' stock sale and the target's deemed asset sale, whereas a 338(h)(10) election typically imposes only one level of tax, which is why it is much more common.
hook: (g) = double; (h)(10) = single.

sources.title: Section 338 - What it is, Implications, S Corporation
sources.quote: In a regular Section 338 election, two levels of tax are imposed: one on the shareholders upon their sale of the target stock and the other on the deemed asset sale by the target corporation (“Old Target”).

sources.title: S Corp Chapter 16 (California Franchise Tax Board)
sources.quote: Therefore, electing IRC Section 338 results in double taxation.

q: By what deadline must a Section 338 election be filed on Form 8023?
a: 15th day of the 9th month after the acquisition date
wrong: With the next annual tax return
explain: Under the statute and IRS instructions, a Section 338 election is due by the 15th day of the 9th month beginning after the month in which the acquisition date occurs.
hook: Nine months, then the 15th.

sources.title: Instructions for Form 8023 (10/2023) | Internal Revenue Service
sources.quote: File Form 8023 by the 15th day of the 9th month after the acquisition date to make a section 338 election for the target corporation.

sources.title: 26 U.S.C. § 338: Certain stock purchases treated as asset acquisitions
sources.quote: Except as otherwise provided in regulations, an election under this section shall be made not later than the 15th day of the 9th month beginning after the month in which the acquisition date occurs.

q: If the offer is $30 of acquirer stock per target share and the acquirer's shares trade at $60, what is the exchange ratio?
explain: Exchange ratio = offer price per target share / acquirer share price = $30 / $60 = 0.5 acquirer shares per target share.
hook: Offer over buyer price.

sources.title: Exchange Ratios in M&A | Fixed vs. Floating Ratio
sources.quote: On January 5, 2014 the target agrees to receive $12 from the acquirer for each of target's 24 million shares (.6667 exchange ratio) upon the completion of the deal

sources.title: Exchange Ratio in M&A Deals: Full Tutorial
sources.quote: But in real life, it's more common to use an Exchange Ratio in 100% Stock deals, where the Seller receives X new shares of the Buyer for each 1 of its own shares.

q: Under a fixed exchange ratio, what is known with certainty at announcement: the number of shares issued or the value received per target share?
explain: With a fixed exchange ratio the share count is locked no matter how share prices move before closing, so the deal value fluctuates with the acquirer's stock price.
hook: Fixed ratio = fixed shares, floating value.

sources.title: Exchange Ratios in M&A | Fixed vs. Floating Ratio
sources.quote: No matter what happens to the target and acquirer share prices between now and February 5, 2014, the share ratio will remain fixed.

sources.title: Exchange Ratio in M&A Deals: Full Tutorial
sources.quote: The most serious problem here is that if the Buyer's Share Price falls, the Seller will get a lower purchase price because the Buyer's shares will be worth less!

q: Which exchange ratio structure guarantees a fixed purchase price while letting the number of shares issued vary?
explain: A floating (fixed-value) exchange ratio converts each target share into however many acquirer shares are needed to equal a predetermined price at closing.
hook: Floating ratio floats so the value can stay put.

sources.title: Exchange Ratio in M&A Deals: Full Tutorial
sources.quote: One solution is to use a Floating Exchange Ratio, which guarantees a fixed Equity Purchase Price, but which allows the number of shares issued to the Seller to vary.

sources.title: Exchange Ratios in M&A | Fixed vs. Floating Ratio
sources.quote: Each target share is converted into the number of acquirer shares that are required to equal the predetermined per-target-share price upon closing.

q: What is the formal name for an earnout in M&A?
explain: An earnout promises future payments to the seller, on top of the upfront payment, if specific milestones such as EBITDA targets are met; it helps bridge valuation gaps.
hook: Earn it out later, contingent on results.

sources.title: Earnouts | M&A Definition + Examples - Wall Street Prep
sources.quote: An earnout, formally called a contingent consideration, is a mechanism used in M&A whereby, in addition to an upfront payment, future payments are promised to the seller upon the achievement of specific milestones (i.e. achieving specific EBITDA targets).
